g.text: How fast each hash runs on aarch64 (Linux), measured 2026-10-02
Hover or tap a dot to compare the hashes there · click a name at right to show or hide it · How to read this graph ▸

g.title: Switch every plot between rate (GB/s, million messages per second) and time (ns per byte, ns per message)
The inputs every plot shows, from smallest (left) to largest; drag an end of the band, or the band itself
Drag to move this end
Drag to move this end
Show every input
Show or hide the plots of messages: one in one buffer now and then, or one after another
Show or hide the plots of batches of 64-byte messages
Show or hide the plots of long messages arriving in 64 KiB pieces
Show or hide the plots of calls each made after the program slept 1 ms, as a server waiting for its next request
Show or hide the plots of calls each made after the program ran other code and read 128 MiB, as a program that hashes between its other tasks
Show or hide the plots of inputs hashed one after another, as fast as the program can
Show or hide nonstop plots where the program hands each buffer over for good and fills the next while it is hashed
Show or hide nonstop plots where the program waits for each call to return before refilling its buffer
Show or hide the nonstop plots of one program hashing alone
Show or hide the nonstop plots of two programs hashing at once

g.text: Each line is one hash. Each dot is the mean of up to 192 timings at that size.
A dot's shape marks the method the hash used at that size. The section "Code paths" at the bottom names each method.
Rate counts bytes or messages per second, time the nanoseconds per byte or message; the switch at right changes every plot.
The strip at the top narrows every plot to part of its inputs: drag an end of its band, or use the arrows at its ends.

After other work: the program calls the hash, runs a fixed other program (about 1 MiB of code) and reads 128 MiB of data, at least 1 ms in all, writes the input, and calls again; the second call is timed. So a program works that hashes between its other tasks.
After idling: the program calls the hash, sleeps 1 ms, writes the input, and calls again; the second call is timed. So a server works that waits for its next request.
Nonstop, each input (each 64 KiB piece of a message in pieces) is first read into memory, a memory copy, the cheapest read, inside the time.
Owned buffers: the program hands each buffer over and fills the next while it is hashed. Lent buffers: the program waits for each call to return before refilling its buffer.
A message in one buffer, after other work
the program hashes, runs other code and reads 128 MiB of memory, and hashes again; the time of the second call
Gigabytes per second (log scale) · higher is better
